utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, before we begin, I just want to update the Chamber regarding the investigation of the threat. With the Court's permission, we had an investigator speak to both Mr. Dulovic and his wife, yesterday and this morning, and the nature of the threat was one phone call to a member of Mr. Dulovic's family, and a threat of a general nature and abusive language. I want to acknowledge the prompt action taken by Minister Mihajlovic and Nenad Milic of the Ministry of Interior. They placed immediate guards around Mr. Dulovic's house and have undertaken an investigation of the matter. And just finally, I would say I'm somewhat concerned about the chilling effect this may have had. It was reported in Belgrade as a threat against Mr. Dulovic, and that has been the reason we went into closed session, and I would invite the Chamber, to the extent it deems appropriate, to publicly recognise Mr. Mihajlovic's commitment to ensuring that any witness who cooperates and appears before the Tribunal will receive adequate protection should they come under threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped at a point when we were dealing with the record of your testimony in court. We say that -- we said, rather, that the perpetrators were treated as persons unknown. And you mentioned a certain Dragica, and then you say, on page 5 of your statement: "I never found out exactly what the last name and first name of that woman were and where she was, but I know that she was very well known at that time in that area of Vukovar." So even as far as this other person is concerned, you don't know yet again who this is. So is there anything unnatural about the fact that the judiciary authorities were instituting proceedings against persons unknown until the identity of the perpetrators was established?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go into that. I said what I had to say, and I abide by that. Everybody knows Dragica. She is from Novi Sad. I don't know what Mr. Sljivancanin said and all the rest, but it was easy to establish who had done this and on whose instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you probably know, Mr. Dulovic, about the explanation that was provided. Actually, this person -- this group of prisoners was taken away by citizens who were armed and who were a furious mob. And nobody justified the fact that they were killed, but weapons were used to seize them from the army, from the guards who were taking care of them, and it wasn't the army that did that. Isn't that clear to you? Or perhaps even that isn't clear to you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to say what is clear to me and what is not clear to me. I said what I learned, what I found out, and I know that for months and months on, these people were free, even after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which people are you talking about? The people from that territory, among whom you mentioned that man from Smederevo when you don't even know exactly who he is, and this woman, and you say that you never managed to find out her first and last name? Are you talking about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones you are talking about, the ones who perpetrated this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it clear that this was not done by Major Sljivancanin or General Mrksic? You say in this statement of yours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're again using this as an opportunity to try and argue your case. It's not for the witness to interpret his evidence; it's for us. Now, you can ask him what these people -- about what these people said, of course, but what is clear or what isn't clear from the evidence is a matter which the Tribunal will have to decide and is not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your statement: "Otherwise I did not see Mrksic during my stay in Vukovar. I heard that he was only in Negoslavci. Also, I never spoke to Sljivancanin about this subject." Do you know, for example, that at the time when these events took place, Mrksic was not even in Slavonia at all, he was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not see Mrksic, that I heard that he was in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, Mr. Dulovic -- let's just see where this is. I have to find your permit to stay in that zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Vukovar one, it's tab -- Exhibit 342, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vukovar, yes. Vukovar. Vukovar, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Here it is. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, please, in this permit of yours, it says that you are allowed to stay there from the 9th of October until the 9th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get the right document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says up here: "Federal Secretariat for National Defence, Department for Instruction and Moral and Ethical Behaviour," and so on and so forth, "Ekspres Politika, Belgrade," and so on and so forth. That's what it says here. So from the 9th of October until the 9th of November; you were allowed to stay there for a month. And you are testifying about a period of time when you were not there; is that right or is that not right, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what's this all about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that at first -- first of all, it says here the permit's validity is extended and is -- and does not only apply to what the federal secretariat granted, and then it is signed Major Petrovic, and there's a stamp. It was possible to travel to Vukovar from May onwards with a journalist's ID only, and then later on, when going there, they required a permit, so that's why I had to get this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dulovic. You made a propaganda film, and then you took some excerpts out of it. When did you make this film?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995 or 1996. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a few years after these events, you made this film, and then you took certain excerpts out of this material. I have the transcript here of that rather unclear footage of that conversation with Sljivancanin. So could you please explain this to me, because I really don't understand what the point is. It says here: "Nicolas Borsinger" -- no. Illegible. And then Sljivancanin: "What's the problem?" And then again NB says: "I'm used to getting better cooperation from the JNA, better than what I'm getting today." Sljivancanin: "Translate this for me: 'Rather than today.' What's this all about?" Then this Borsinger says: "The colonel is aware of all the problems." Sljivancanin: "Well, there are no problems. Only --" and then there's nothing more. And then he says: "The colonel is here." Sljivancanin: "I just know that some civilians --" and then the rest is inaudible. The Colonel: "What's the problem? The problem -- Point out what the problem is. Point out what the problem is." Borsinger says: "That's where I can see the soldiers walking down the street. I can see trucks getting in. Look there. Look there." Sljivancanin says: "Well, now I've opened the bridge for traffic." Colonel: "So that bridge was not open for traffic." Sljivancanin: "Because I heard there was shooting there. It was closed for traffic because there was shooting there. Did you hear about this, sir?" Borsinger: "My colleagues were there." Sljivancanin: "Sir, if you're interested only in the fate of these people who were in the basement and who are provided security for by my soldiers, they are taken care of." He says: "They are taken care of. And if you're not interested in the fact that my young soldiers are getting killed, those who are 18, 19, 20 years old, then you are not welcome here. And sir, my own soldiers were killed here tonight. And sir, there is a war going on here." Borsinger: "I know." Sljivancanin: "And we are trying to make sure that all of you are safe and that peace is secured for you, while you come to me talking of problems. If you don't like it here, feel free to go to where you like it. And I'm very embarrassed for you to treat me this way. Whatever you asked of me, I have given you." What are you proving with this? What are you proving with this episode from this film? What's this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a proper question. That is a matter --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a matter for the Court, to determine what is proved. But what the witness can deal with is the circumstances in which this conversation took place. What was happening, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the accused has confused this film. I did not participate in it. He didn't listen carefully when the matter was discussed in this courtroom. This is an excerpt from a different kind of footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm talking about this excerpt that you showed of Sljivancanin. So I want this footage. It doesn't matter whether it's from that film. This is what you provided. So what is the point? What is the point of presenting this conversation? Because I don't see anything in this conversation that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, that's a matter for argument. You can argue that to us. The witness can't answer the question. It's merely some footage which has been provided. But tell us, please, remind us, if you would, Mr. Dulovic: What was happening that morning between the Red Cross and Major Sljivancanin? Can you help us to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. First of all, I did not participate in the filming that is being referred to now. This was filmed by another crew, a TV crew. I listened to Mr. Sljivancanin, and I still have a few sentences when he was giving these explanations to the gentlemen from the Red Cross, that he would not let him in because this is a war zone and there's a war going on and there are armed Ustashas there, and something to that effect. As for this part, I was not there next to him when he said what is recorded in this particular footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when -- just a moment. To clarify matters, when you say he wouldn't let the Red Cross in, where were the Red Cross seeking access to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very entrance into the hospital. So not in the hospital, but this is in front of the entrance into the hospital, about five or six metres in front. This is a different scene, the one that is referred to here in this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say, Mr. Dulovic, that this scene that is recorded here has nothing to do with what you've been testifying about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It does have something to do with it. This lasted much longer. I simply said what I heard when he was speaking. He was shouting, Major Sljivancanin was, quite a bit, on that occasion. As for the details of his conversation with the gentleman from the Red Cross, I am not aware of them, but he was shouting this for the sake of the public, because there were quite a few journalists around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was shouting for the sake of the public and explaining that his soldiers were being killed and that he did everything that he asked him to do?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go back to what I mentioned, your film. Since you made that propaganda film in 1995, as you put it yourself --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That question involved an implied criticism, it may be, and you should have the chance to deal with it. What is said is that it was a propaganda film. Is that a true characterisation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I see this film here. I first saw this film here, or rather, this particular scene. Perhaps it was broadcast on television too, but I don't know. I don't know who recorded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding, which I could quite understand. As I understand the accused, he's talking about the longer film which you made, or we were told you had made, about the Yellow Wasps. I think that's what he's talking about. He was describing it as a propaganda film.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, that's not true. What I saw was the truth, and also what I saw in the courtroom when the trial of the Yellow Wasps was held. And then there's also the interview of Vojin Vuckovic, and these other scenes. As for this part, I didn't work on it. This was taken by the director from some other material that had been made public. So I did not discuss the subject with him, this particular excerpt that refers to Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, you are testifying about some cooperation of mine in 1991 and 1992 with Vojislav Seselj. As you know, he was in opposition. So I would like you to comment for me upon this letter that I got through my associates. It has to do with you and also your predecessor from the same news magazine. I'm not going to read the whole thing, although it's a one-page letter, and it's handwritten, so it's basically one third of a typewritten page. It says: "Both of them are invoking some alleged statements of mine post festum. Possibly given during the time of a fierce propaganda war between the Serb Radical Party and the Socialist Party of Serbia in intervals between my two stints in prison. Such statements, where the passionate protagonists of a political conflict are competing in mutual accusations can never be a source of the truth." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And then it says: "Mr. Milosevic, I remind you that you and I first net on the 27th of February, 1992, at the meeting of the National Assembly of Serbia and we only shook hands then," which is true. When I came to parliament, I shook hands with the people who were closest to me physically around there. I shook hands with the MPs who were around me. And then I quote: "We did not talk." Of course, that's true. "Our first conversation was in May 1992, namely, about the coming federal elections. We never discussed war operations or sending volunteers. The Serb radical party directly sent all its volunteers to JNA units and they all met up at the Bubanj Potok barracks. All these volunteers were regular soldiers of the JNA and their service in wartime was recorded in their military IDs. A smaller number of volunteers was within the Territorial Defence of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, and later on in the army of Republika Srpska. The Srpska Radical Party never had any paramilitary formations. I am prepared, Mr. Milosevic, to testify truthfully about all wartime events, and I'm surprised that The Hague Prosecutor considers me to be inaccessible. As soon as I get official summons, I'm coming. Respectfully yours, Vojislav Seselj." Signed yesterday. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what Vojislav Seselj says in a letter. I don't suppose the witness can comment on it, but we will ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two things: One, I would ask that that letter be marked, and if Mr. Milosevic doesn't wish to introduce it into evidence, the Prosecution would ask that it be preserved. One, for two reasons: I believe it is an important piece of evidence, in and of itself. Secondly, I'm quite concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I must tell you, it hasn't been our practice so far to exhibit the various statements which Mr. Milosevic has relied on, for the very good reason that they're not evidence; they're merely material which he's putting forward. And the danger of doing it, if I may say, is that you may want to have this one marked, but there may be a great many which you wouldn't wish to have marked as evidence. Anyway, we'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The point I wish to make, Your Honour, regarding this particular piece is I'm concerned that how did Mr. Seselj know what this witness testified to yesterday when it was a closed session? That piece of video was shown in closed session, and now we have a response from Mr. Seselj 24 hours later. That causes me some concern, especially in the light of events of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, can you help us to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please, Mr. May. First of all, I will answer your questions only when I am a witness, but I will answer now. Please respect your own rules. For the sake of brevity, I did not read out the beginning. It says: "Dear Mr. Milosevic, I am amazed by the false testimony of two journalists of the journal Vreme, Dejan Anastasijevic and Jovan Dulovic. They showed themselves long ago to be agents of Western intelligence services." Then he goes on to say what I quoted. They both refer to statements I allegedly made post festum which I may have made at the time of a fierce propaganda war. This was a major clash between the Socialist Party and the Serb Radical Party. They were attacking me, and of course he wanted to harm me, harm me as much as he could with these statements. So this is what he says, referring to both witnesses. And what is important here is that there is no basis for the stories they tell about volunteers and so on. I saw this man for the first time only a year later, and we talked for the first time even longer after that, and the topic of our conversation was the elections. We never discussed -- no one from the government ever discussed from anyone from the opposition whether they were sending volunteers or not. This refers to both witnesses, and I can give you this letter for you to look at. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was this part in open session, what Seselj said?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this video was played towards the end of the direct examination yesterday, during closed session. I can check, Your Honour, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was done on 16th of October, day 110, and I guess it was in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first video, I know, was played -- the Vukovar video was played the first day. I will check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was the Seselj video, which came towards the end of his evidence, if my recollection is right, which suggests it was in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well, Your Honour. I can check my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the page 11680.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the registrar points out that the exhibit may have been public, and was public, and wasn't under seal. Now, that may be right. But let us not spend time on this now. It's something which can be determined. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. The application is that this should be a document which is exhibited. So the first question is for you, Mr. Milosevic: Do you object to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to Seselj's letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. You can have it. You can have it. Of course you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. Before we deal with it, we'll decide whether to admit it or not. Mr. Dulovic, you've been sitting there patiently while all this has been going on. Is there anything you would like to say about what's been read out to you? You should have the opportunity to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. First of all, this film was a documentary film. It was made as a documentary film. Secondly, when we are talking about the army and about volunteers, I wish to tell you that I investigated this, and I know for certain that members of the Radical Party, of Mr. Seselj's party, volunteered. They volunteered in their local Radical Party boards, where lists were drawn up. Then these lists of names were sent to the republic Ministry of the Interior, the police, to be checked. I don't know what sort of check exactly it was, whether they checked whether these people had criminal records or whether it was something else that was checked. After this, the lists were sent back to the municipal boards, which then sent call-up notes to those volunteers who had been accepted. After this, the volunteers went to military training ground near Belgrade, called Bubanj Potok, where they were trained for a time. They were trained as soldiers, they received military training. From there, the state transported them to wherever they were needed as soldiers, and then they were issued with weapons. What I saw is, for example, an event in Vukovar, where this man Kameni was. He was the leader of one such unit which was stationed nearby, but it had its own command, its own leader. When needed, however, they were used for certain operations. This does not mean, by any means, that they did not act independently, without any control by the army, for example, to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I forgot to mention that these people never underwent any kind of medical examination, so that I am sure that I saw men who were -- who would never have been accepted in a regular army after a psychiatric check-up. There were people like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, you could have seen anyone in the war theatre, but if you're talking about volunteers who joined the Yugoslav National Army, then they were soldiers of the JNA and not paramilitary formations. And Mr. Seselj says here: "The Serbian Radical Party never had paramilitary formations."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You probably know better. I'm just saying what he writes here. Do you remember that the standpoint taken by our country was always categorically against any sort of paramilitary units because we considered them to be thieves, looters, and not military units?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear in mind that we've wasted a lot of time, quite unnecessarily, with these discussions which were not initiated by me, so please take account of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're not going to get away with that. These kind of comments are wholly out of order. These are important issues which you raised, you read out Seselj's letter. You can't then be surprised when it's clarified. You may not like the answers, but they're the answers which the witness has given. Now, the Chamber will consider whether we're going to exhibit this particular letter or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to admit this letter, but we are going to mark it for identification since there is an issue as to whether it was or was not obtained in circumstances or sent in circumstances when evidence was adduced in closed session. Now, it may or -- that may or may not be the case, but the upshot is that we will exhibit it, but for that -- I mean mark it for identification, but for that limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked for identification as Defence Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't want to waste time. I asked my associates to ask Mr. Seselj where and when he gave such an interview, which must be false because he couldn't have talked about this; I never even knew the man at the time. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we shall have [Previous translation continues]... the evidence. If you want to add anything else, do, by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm saying there's no need to investigate whether it was in open or closed session. It was in closed session yesterday, but I was amazed that someone could talk such nonsense, so I asked that this be checked, whether Seselj ever gave such an interview or not. And you've heard his explanation. At the time when there were clashes between the Socialist Party and the Serbian Radical Party, when he, as a politician, thought it was not his duty to tell the truth but to harm his opponent as much as possible, that's when he said this. And it's true that at the time I didn't even know him. He goes on to say that they never had paramilitary units. So what I said, Mr. May, about the time is not because I don't like the witness's replies, but because I don't want us to waste too much time which will then prevent me from putting other questions to the witness. My remark was about the time and not about what the witness was saying, and it's obviously what sort of things he's saying. That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, please, you returned to Belgrade after this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the registrar say something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked for identification as D55, but it will also be under seal, confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel I must just note for the record that it seems what Mr. Milosevic has just told us is that after the events of yesterday morning, after this man expressing fear that some of the people he would testify about yesterday were the ones he feared the most, to then take information from a closed session and communicate that to the very person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't interpret it that way, and I'm not going to go into an examination now. It's perfectly possible that he spoke to his associates at the end of the first day, which, of course, was in open Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, whatever happened and whatever kind of session, I suppose I have the right to ask someone who is said to have said something, whether he actually said it and whether this is true or not. I suppose I have that right. It's not about Dulovic or anything else; it's about an interview given by a man who was then asked what this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, you say -- or rather, you mentioned first one person and then another person, in connection with the events in Vukovar and Ovcara, and after that, you returned to Belgrade. It doesn't matter what day it was, but after five, ten, or fifteen days - it doesn't matter - you returned to Belgrade. When you came back to Belgrade, did you go to report what you saw and heard to anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic, but as a journalist reporting on the courts and the judiciary, you should have known that you were supposed to report this to some sort of organ.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These organs were in the field. It would have been stupid for me to go and report something that the people who were in charge of this could have seen for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think the army had anything to do with these events?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anything. I'm just saying what I saw. My personal opinion is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say, in the last passage, that an order came that all volunteers should be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. You should read this more carefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here is the last paragraph, page 6: "On the following day, an order was issued to all volunteers to hand in their weapons."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The Vukovar operation was over. They were no longer needed. They handed back their weapons and returned home. So it was not that they were disarmed but that they returned the weapons they had been issued. But this has nothing to do with the event in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I connected it with this because in the next passage after the one where you mention Ovcara, you say: "On the following day, an order was put out for all volunteers to hand in their weapons."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two things have no connection with each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vukovic [as interpreted], I'm just reading out from your statement. I suppose that this was a response by these organs in the field to what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your assumption is wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that this was not so?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because all the units all around Vukovar, even those that had nothing to do with Ovcara, had to hand their weapons back because they were no longer needed. There was no longer any fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's what you're explaining now, but your statement says something different.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say something different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to save time, you spoke about an exchange. Do you know about an exchange that took place in March 1992, when 41 persons were taken over from the Croatian side and they were exchanged for a group of 380 members of the paramilitary formations of Croatia because the army at that time agreed to accept this exchange all for all, and that this exchange took place at the end of March 1992? Do you know what was done with these people who had been taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to ask you about that, then. They were mostly civilians. Some of them were women. The youngest person was 24, the oldest one was 73. I'm not going to read you all this, but it would be a good thing if you acquainted yourself with the matter. Perhaps it would be more difficult for you to speak about the good treatment that the Serbs were accorded in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said; that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dulovic. Of three -- if you have three witnesses of one event, you will get three different descriptions of the event, and I'm sure you know that as a journalist attending court cases. But we have very little time, so I'll have to focus on the part of your statement relating to Bosnia. You followed the events in Zvornik, and you explained that you came to Zvornik, that it was dangerous when you arrived, and that you went back to Mali Zvornik straight away. And you say that, over there, there were paramilitaries stationed for the most part. You go on to say that afterwards - so the 10th of May - there was a plaque reading "Republika Srpska" on it, and on the bridge there were members of the regular federal police force and the police force of the Republic of Serbia. The police of the Republic of Serbia, I assume you saw just at the border crossing. Is that right, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said: The members of the police force of Republika Srpska, you were able to see only along the border crossing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that was the border crossing where I had seen them, then that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the bridge over the River Drina between Mali Zvornik and Veliki Zvornik. Mali Zvornik is in Serbia and the other Zvornik - it's not called Big Zvornik, it's just Zvornik - that's in Bosnia, right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware that that was a border crossing, nor did anybody ask me for my passport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Not to say the border crossing. What I'm talking about is the bridge between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was only on that bridge that you were able to see policemen belonging to the police force of the Republic of Serbia. I assume you didn't see them in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I couldn't have seen those people who were on the bridge over there in Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you see any policemen of the Republic of Serbia on the other side, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in uniform?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean our own policemen, policemen from Serbia. Did you see them in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to -- that's what I want to clear up. They were on the territory of Serbia, which it is their job to be, and you say that they didn't allow anybody crossing in with weapons. What else could they have done?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's absolutely right. There's nothing that I challenge there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn at the time that they told you in Serbia that there were a lot of criminals and bandits in Zvornik and that it was very dangerous for you to go there at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it logical, then, that the police force on the bridge from Serbia, on a bridge linking Serbia to Bosnia, where there was a great deal of violence, would prevent anybody entering carrying weapons? And regardless of the fact that Yugoslavia was still in existence, you didn't need a passport, you're quite right there, but the police does have the discretionary right to prevent anybody from passing if they consider them to be suspect and ask what they want to do in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite right, but there's a very significant detail here. They didn't allow Vojin Vuckovic and his own people, that is to say, Seselj's unit, for whom you say yourself was under the auspices of the JNA. So that particular unit, whether they were looters or not, they were registered as a unit called the Yellow Wasps, led by Major Dusan Vojin Vuckovic, who, as he told me, was an instructor in the federal police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Dulovic. I did not tell you that he was under the patronage of the JNA. The federal police force arrested members of these Yellow Wasps. Do you know that? Do you know that the police actually arrested any member of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a long time after the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me how long after?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, several years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this trial of Vuckovic's was in 1996; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the trial was in 1996, I suppose you assume that it was because somebody just took it into his mind for political reasons in 1996 to launch proceedings and bring the person to trial; is that your explanation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My explanation is that what they wanted was to show that we in Serbia were capable of bringing war criminals to trial. And that was a complete fiasco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this -- somebody suddenly took this into their minds in 1996; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dulovic. I have here -- it says "The Republic of Serbia." This is a court file. The Republic of Serbia, the district public prosecutor. The town is Sabac, because that's where it took place. The investigating judge of the district court in Sabac. And then it says: "Criminal Report, Vuckovic Dusko, nicknamed Repic, from Umka, and Vuckovic Vojin, from Umka, et cetera, et cetera, who their mother and father was, and then why the accusations are being made, what the charges are. And it says: "During the civil war in the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, violating the laws of international warfare during the war, perpetrated killings and torture of the civilian population." And then it goes on to state the following: "On the 10th of June, 1992, in the cultural centre in Celopek where a large number of civilians were being detained from Divice. He tortured these individuals by organising a box match between these individuals, promising that the stronger one would be spared his life." And then Cikaric Enes from Divice as well, he cut off his ear and then proceeded to shoot from a small-calibre pistol at these persons. Some of them were killed on the spot and others were wounded. He would pierce their hearts and kill them in that way. So that he killed, in total, 17 persons, and these persons, it says here, were then transported by him to the quarry and took another four individuals to load out the bodies, and he killed those four persons too from a small-calibre rifle. So he stands accused of 21 murders and previous tortures of these same individuals. I assume that you know all about that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it in all its details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears that there's just one small point that seems to have elapsed -- that seems to have escaped you in what you have said. The date is 1993. The year is 1993, Mr. Dulovic, and not 1996. Because nobody took it into their minds to do this in 1996, to bring people to justice. The date on this document is 1993, and I tender it into evidence. Not only is this correct, but the reliability of this witness is brought into question because he claims that this was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I thought it was in 1996 because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please take this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that point, as to the significance of 1993 and 1996. Yes. Let the document be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the point is not even in that particular matter of whether it was 1996 or 1993. It speaks of the exactness of the testimony, and in Serbia, war crimes were prosecuted. It was not that the crimes were made little of. It says that he killed 17 persons, plus the other four that helped him carry the dead bodies. It specifies the torture that he resorted to. So it is quite obvious that nobody wanted to hide anything when it comes to criminals of this type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Defence Exhibit D56, under seal, confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clear this up. So you saw the Yellow Wasps. They were an ordinary paramilitary unit which had nothing to do with either the army or the police force of Republika Srpska or the army of Republika Srpska; is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that they were wearing regular camouflage uniforms, all of them were armed, and they looked like an official army except for their long hair, untidy hair, and things like that, and the caps they wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dulovic. I have understood you to say that the Serbs over there had taken control of Zvornik and that there was no violence committed and that they weren't in any danger. That was what you wanted to say in your testimony, as far as I understood you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. That's not right. That's not what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me: How did the clash come about in Zvornik to begin with, and whether you know anything at all about the violence that was committed against the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina after those decisions to leave behind Cutilheiro's plan, and after the Croatian regular army had crossed the River Sava, stormed the area after the killing of civilians by the Croatian and Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there when it all began, nor do I know what you're talking about. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to mention just something with respect to the Zvornik municipality, which is where you were and what you're testifying about, and I'm also going to mention, as this is a long list of persons killed, I'm going to mention just the women and only the women who were killed during the period of time that you yourself were there, Mr. Dulovic. For example: Stojanka Grujic, Gornje Bajlkovice, the Zvornik municipality, husband's name Uros, born in 1936, killed at the beginning of May, 1992. You arrived on the 10th. She was killed on the 9th, when the Muslim army stormed her village. The body was found lying by the house in which she lived. Then again, the next one, Mica Zaric, 56 years of age, killed on the 6th of May, when the Muslims attacked Gornje Baljkovica. Then again, Ulika Kojic was killed, 67 years old, also at the beginning of May 1992. Then the next one is N. Mitrovic. She was killed. Her husband's name was Bora, from the Srpski Nezuk village of the Zvornik municipality, on the 6th of May, 1992, by members of the Muslim armed forces. Then we have Ljeposava Mitrovic, 45 years old, also killed on the 6th of May by the Muslim forces in the village of Gornji Ba. And so on and so on. So I'm just reading the names of the women who were killed. Another one here: N. Savic, the wife of Milos Savic from the village of Boskovici in the municipality of Zvornik, killed on the 5th of May, 1992, when the Muslims attacked her village. Savic Simka from Gornje Baljkovica, 65 years of age, killed on the 9th of May when the Muslims attacked her village. There are many other women here on this list. I can't read them all out. And on this list of persons killed, men, there are 118 who were killed in the Zvornik municipality alone, in which you claim that it was the Serbs who attacked the innocent Muslims and then caused a war of some kind to break out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... all he's describing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you see any of these women killed, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This happened in some villages that -- I wasn't in those villages. I was in quite another place, not where these people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dulovic. I'm telling you, for example, that we have here -- there are a lot of them, but I have 118 names of Serbs who were killed in the Zvornik municipality. I understood you to say that the Serbs went there to kill the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you say that, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Dulovic, of anyone, any one of these killers on the Muslim side, did you ever hear of any one of them, and did you hear about the crimes that they had committed over the Serbian population in the Zvornik municipality? Because you're talking about Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the town of Zvornik, not the Zvornik municipality, because the municipality includes the villages, and I'm only talking about a part of the town of Zvornik, at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have a whole list of people who were killed in Zvornik proper, lots of them too. But what I'm asking you is whether you heard anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here 38 names of the perpetrators of crimes against Serbs in the municipality of Zvornik alone, but as you have not heard about any of this, what about Hajrudin Mesic, nicknamed Labud, from Teocak, who organised the killing of civilians in the Zvornik municipality between May 1992 and August 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. It would take too long to read out all 38 names. You say you haven't heard about any people who committed crimes in the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not something that was talked about at the time. Perhaps later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Dulovic, you are claiming, you are asserting, that the Muslim crimes in the Zvornik municipality that you are testifying about were the fruits of Serbian propaganda that the papers wrote about and not the facts that I am bringing to light here before you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... where did the witness say that? What part of his evidence are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I heard him say into the microphone, here in this courtroom - I can't quote the line now or passage of his testimony - but I heard him say that there was nothing there, actually; it was just all Serbian propaganda and the way they wanted to incite the war there, fan the flames of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This isn't limited to Zvornik; you're now talking generally, are you? That -- because it's right that he did give evidence about Serb propaganda, generally, and its incitement. What he said was it was inciting people, or that was the effect of it, to war, or inciting fear in them, and it was all propaganda. Now, you want to ask him a question about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I cannot understand that to incite people, if you publish the killing of elderly persons, women, children, civilians, peasants, farmers. The papers are free entities, they can publish what they like. Is there anybody who can order a paper not to publish and print what it likes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His evidence was, Mr. Milosevic, that there were stories which were untrue which were being published. If you want to ask him about that, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked him a question. I said: How can he claim that there -- that all this did not happen, everything that I am reading out now, and that it was all the fruit of Serb fabrications, when matters were actually quite different, the situation was quite different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite the wrong interpretation of what I had been saying. I did not deny -- I just say I don't know about the victims that you have just spoken about. When I spoke about propaganda, I spoke in general terms about the propaganda that was being launched. It was euphoric. I don't want to quote examples now, but lots of things were written in the papers. They said that in Bosnia the animals in zoos were being fed with Serb children, babies, and that people were killed -- children were killed because there was a lack of oxygen in other places. And large-scale fabrications of this kind to incite and nurture nationalistic feelings, extreme nationalistic feelings, which brought us to what we all know happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, you know that our policies and politics were quite different. Let me quote an example from the area you were in. Do you know that in Mali Zvornik, which means on the territory of Serbia, across the Drina River, and you said that it was 50 metres wide at that time --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't measure the river, but that's it about, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mali Zvornik, if the Drina is 50 metres wide - it could be 150 metres, it doesn't matter how wide the Drina River is at that particular point - but the time that you're talking about, there were 20 per cent Muslims living there. The population in Mali Zvornik was 20 per cent Muslim. And that this figure was never reduced. On the contrary; it increased, because some Muslims had crossed over onto the territory of Serbia, and nothing ever happened to a single Muslims on Serbian territory. And the number of Muslims in Mali Zvornik today is greater than it was ten years ago. And the figure was greater in 1996 as well. Once the peace had been signed in Dayton in 1995, there were more Muslims than there were in 1991, in fact, when the war began there. Do you know about that? Are you aware of that, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't say that that is not the case, but I'm not aware of it. I'm hearing this for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how, then, is it possible and what was the cause of that, that only a few hundred metres across the Drina, Serbs should be setting fire to Muslim houses, whereas this was never attempted in the Republic of Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all argument from you, and you do this all the time. The witnesses give their evidence of what they saw and heard, and you try and argue with them, and it's all a waste of time, a waste of the Court's time. Now, ask him about his evidence, what he saw and heard. That's what he's giving evidence about, not your arguments about why the Serbs were doing all this and why the Muslims were. He's not given evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness said here and now, if you were listening to him, two minutes ago, that what had been organised was a media campaign of inciting hatred against the Muslims, which is a flagrant lie, because had there been such a campaign, how would he explain the fact that 50 metres across the Drina no Muslim was hurt in any way and that the number of Muslims even went up rather than down over those ten years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask him about the campaign instead of arguing about it. That is what he says about it, that this was a propaganda campaign in which lies were told and fabrications were uttered in order to incite the population. Now, if you say it's not true, if you say, for instance, that there was no -- just a moment. If you say there was no story that the animals were fed with children, this kind of thing, if you say it's not true, challenge it. Put it to the witness it's not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the newspapers from all sides wrote all kinds of despicable things. I'm not going into all of that. I'm just asking him whether he can put these facts into a logical context in relation to his assertion that there was warmongering against the Muslims, and nothing happened to Muslims in Serbia during the war. As a matter of fact, Mr. May, we took in 70.000 Muslim refugees from Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did answer. He said no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you put a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer was no. I have another one.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first one where you said that I said no, what did I say? Can I read this? What is this that you asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's not go over this again. Mr. Milosevic, no wonder the witness -- the witness is confused. Now, have you another question for him? Let's get on to another topic. Time is short.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you -- I'm reading from the transcript now - I asked you precisely about that, that there was no propaganda against the Muslims because nothing happened to a single Muslim Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in Serbia, because had there been propaganda, then something would have happened to them. And as a matter of fact, we took in 70.000 Muslim refugees from Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point of repeating what you've already said and making a speech?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've been told more than once: The purpose of cross-examination is not to argue your case. You can do that in due course. But not to waste the Court's time by constant argument. Now, have you questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, do you know that in the area around Mali Zvornik -- I'm talking about the territory of the Republic of Serbia now. And I consider myself to be responsible for that, that is to say, the territory of Serbia. I was president of Serbia. That in the area around Mali Zvornik are a few villages that are purely Muslim, and in them, no one was ever disturbed, although the Drina is only 50 metres wide, and on the other side there was a civil war that was raging?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in Mali Zvornik there is also a mosque, because Muslims live there, and that this mosque was never damaged or were ugly words written on it, or was it threatened in any other way? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there is a mosque there. It was guarded by policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you find this logical, that they had to guard it? Because fifty metres away, on the other side, there were grave killings and there was unrest.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said what I saw. It's not for me to think this or that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Dulovic. Did you know anything, for example, about the attack of the Muslim armed forces on the village of Gornja Kamenica and the killing of a large number of people, and that this attack was led by Esad Mehmedovic, a former policeman, Meho Suljagic, Edo Hazkic [phoen], and Esad and Ahmed Grebic? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no idea where Kamenica is, or was I ever there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened at the road between Zvornik and Sehovici, when the Muslim forces attacked a column of vehicles in which there were Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twelve of them were killed then. Inter alia, a pregnant woman was heavily wounded. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the attack? I mean, all of these are villages around Zvornik. They are very close to Zvornik. The village of Gornja Baljkovica, also the municipality of Zvornik, 14 civilians, Serb civilians, were killed. I have their names. I'm not going to read them out. Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, there was looting and their cattle were taken away, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I was not there in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about Snagovo and the large-scale killings of civilians by Muslim forces there, and also the castration of some men and torture, mutilation, and also other things also around Zvornik? Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in Zvornik for a very short while, so I did not have the opportunity of hearing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear, for example, of the killing of Mihajlo Pantic, a Serb who was 90 years old? He was killed by three bullets.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about that, because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear anything about killings in the municipality of Zvornik that were committed? Did you hear about what was done by units that were commanded by Naser Oric from Srebrenica and how many slaughters they committed in the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, for example, you say that on the 10th of May you were in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, there was a large-scale massacre of the civilian population. There, right in front of Zvornik, in the village of Boskovici, Mitra Gajic was killed, Stanka Spasojevic -- these are women, for those who are not familiar with the names. They don't know that these are women's names. Draga Lukic. Dragana Cvijetic, Milosava Kostic, Draga Tesic, and so on. Many women among the killed. See, on the 5th of May. You did not hear about any of this and you were in Zvornik on the 10th of May, five days after that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is logical that I would not hear anything. News went slowly. People were busy with their own affairs, and I did not hear about that. That was not the subject then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What was the subject, if it wasn't crimes? Look at this, please. In the month of April - let's go a month back - before you came to Zvornik. When did you first come to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says when I came. It says so over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't find it. Now, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said so the other day, but I had the papers with me. I can't remember now. I don't know. I think that again it was the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 10th of April, and this is the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it so happened, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 10th of May was his answer. Yes, let's move on. It's not a memory test here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not testing the witness's memory. I just can't find it here in my notes when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, I have here material about things that happened on the 17th of April, 1992, very grave events, a very large number of people were killed. This is the municipality of Zvornik, the village of Rastusnica. Did you hear anything about this attack of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. At that time, when I was in Zvornik, what was topical was the clash between the commander of the Territorial Defence and a strong paramilitary formation, the man who led such a formation, and he said that he was one of Seselj's men, this was this Cele. That was the topical thing going on there at that time. I could not sit there and talk to someone about something that was going on. This was more urgent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What is more urgent, Mr. Dulovic, than such mass killings of civilians throughout the municipality of Zvornik? Don't tell me it's more urgent whether one hoodlum is quarrelling with another one. You said that you had lunch with this man for several hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that that was the most urgent thing you should deal with, to have lunch with him for several hours so that you would discuss these matters with him? All of it was more urgent than what I'm quoting to you now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was more urgent for me was to find out what was going on in Zvornik and who was who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you really think that such a source could be reliable, or do you assume that this source wanted to tell you his own story, and he thinks that that's the way it suits him? Can you really take such a criminal as a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just conveyed what he had said to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Dulovic. I'm not asking you about these individual names. I told you how many were involved. But I'm asking you about all of this. Did you ever get any information about the large number of civilians who were killed in the municipality of Zvornik? So let us leave the names aside, the actual names, the number of women involved, et cetera. Did you ever find out anything about this? Did you ever write about the civilian casualties in the municipality of Zvornik or about the perpetrators of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by the local correspondents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correspondents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you a correspondent of Ekspres Politika then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was a journalist at the editorial desk. Correspondents are people who are local correspondents in various towns in Serbia, throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But when, as a journalist from the desk, you go, and when you're in the field and then you're a kind of special reporter from the spot, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could put it that way, but it really depends on the subject involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what was the subject involved? What was your topic at the time when you were in Zvornik; to discuss who was against who with these criminals or to see what was actually going on?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my affair and the affair of the editors. They decided to go and find out what was going on in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever find anything out about the mass graves in the municipality of Zvornik, 15 kilometres to the south, in the region of the village of Kamenica? Did you ever hear anything about this, let alone write about it? I assume you never did.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about it, and I was never there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Dulovic. You explained here, as a matter of fact for quite a long period of time, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was a member of the federal Ministry of the Interior, and as proof of that, you mentioned that at the trial that you attended, some certificate was shown concerning a loan, and now that was supposed to be confirmation of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, belonging to the federal Ministry of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then also there was a lot of bidding here, and then the figure reached was many thousands of dollars. During those years, in the 1980s, the rate of exchange varied, but at that time it was probably 3.000 dinars for one dollar. So it was probably about 3.000 dollars, this entire amount of 9 million dinars. Why would I waste time with that now, when you can check it with the exchange rates lists that were published by all newspapers in those days at that time? So you can get information about this. Do you know who the Minister of the Interior was during the 1980s in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that it was Stane Dolanc, the leading Slovenian in those days? He headed the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now time to adjourn. Before we do, Mr. Groome, can you just help us with this: We have a number of motions concerning a Witness 36. I don't think he's on the list, but it would be helpful to know when it's anticipated he's to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we anticipate calling him either the 29th or 30th of this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So he's not immediate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May, in relation to that, could I just say something? I do not have any kind of list of coming witnesses except for the next two. I only know about the next two witnesses. One is what's his name, (redacted)the one who comes after this witness, and the one after that is some (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, can you get -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Groome, the accused should have a longer list. Can you make sure he gets one today to cover all next week and as far ahead as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me conclude, then. We broke off when you said that Zeljko Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Raznjatovic, Arkan, used to be an employee of the federal Ministry of the Interior and that this was in the 1980s, or rather, that there was a trial then, and before that, he had been an employee. So what? So what if he was an employee of the Ministry of the Interior in the 1980s? So what? What meaning does it have? What significance does it have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is for us to say, whether it has any significance at all, not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember that at the time, this same Ministry of the Interior was headed by Stane Dolanc, the leading Slovenian in the then Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you were asked whether Vuckovic - is that the man, Cele?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Vuckovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojin Vuckovic was -- and his brother, Dusan Vuckovic, they had a military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. I only want to clarify one point. You were asked whether he had anything to do with the official authorities, the government authorities of Yugoslavia or Serbia, and to that question, you replied that he used to be employed as an instructor for the marshal arts in the federal SUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this indicate a connection? For example, an English teacher in the federal SUP or some other teacher - for physical education, for example, the martial arts, English, French, maths, for example - is that supposed to indicate that he had some sort of connection with the authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that a male nurse, for example, employed in a state hospital, has something to do with the state organs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The comparison is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic. Apart from the fact that he was a martial arts instructor once upon a time, you don't know anything else about any connection of his with the government authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my observations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did you observe him to have connections to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Sabac authorities, when he was tried there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was that connection?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He approached the president of the chamber and throughout the trial, the two were whispering to each other, which was unprecedented in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the man sentenced?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was given a suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean he's not in prison?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojin Vuckovic was not imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man who killed 17 people; is that who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to Vojin Vuckovic's elder brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in the one who was accused of murder.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the one who was accused of 17 murders?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sentenced to seven years in prison in the first instance. I don't know whether he's still in prison or whether he's in prison at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know what the final judgement was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say -- when you were asked how you came by your information, I noted down your answer. You said that you found out from people whom you assumed would know. That was what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that information gathered by such means, from people whom you assume know something, can be taken as some sort of serious information-gathering?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on my judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider that when you are interviewing a criminal, such as Cele, and he tells you something, that this is valid information?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I think so, yes. He was very convincing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you assume that someone who kills and loots, don't you think that he might also lie, or do you think that he kills and loots but he speaks the truth?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at one point, and you were referring to your trip to Uzice, who was there with you? What other journalists were with you when you were going to Zvornik and Visegrad? What other journalists were there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bojana Marjanovic, a colleague of mine.
