utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only she?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You marked on a map the place from which you say you saw fires burning on the other bank of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic. Do you know, because you passed along that way, that on the other side of the Drina there are high hills and a lot of woodland, and that you could not have seen those fires, by any means, from the place you marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in assuming that later on you visited those areas and established what had happened where, and not that you saw fires at the time? That was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible, and what I said is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there's a lot of smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you can see on your map what the distance is. You can see how many hills lie between the village you speak about and the spot.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villages were named for me by people standing on the bank of the Drina, on the Serbian side, and observing all this. When I asked them what was going on, they told me the names of those villages: Redzici, Djapici, Krasno Polje, Rzine, and Lonjin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this map which I'm looking at is a sign you made, and on the side you were looking at, there are some hundred villages, only on this map that you provided, and this village of Redzici is in the middle of the map. Is this what you're talking about, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This village was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you claim that from there you were able to see the fire in Redzici very well.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. That's what you're saying now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't me who brought this map. It wasn't me who explained that Redzici was set on fire and that it is from this spot that you saw the fire.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw fires. I do not know the area. I asked people what was going on there, and they told me the villages that I have just named are on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic. That's enough for us to estimate the reliability of what you said.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are people who have farms there and who are familiar with every house, let alone every village on the other side of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see how many kilometres there are between that spot and Redzici?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's over hill tops?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic. Just one question about what you said about your notes on what Seselj said when he was in Vukovar. Did you publish an article about this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that if you were keeping notes, you did that in order to write something later on. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't remember whether I mentioned that detail in my text. I would have to check it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say that the newspaper -- or rather, that the policy was to cleanse the army of non-Serbian staff. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. You would have to read this for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said during the examination-in-chief - I don't know where exactly - that there was a tendency to cleanse the army of non-Serbian members. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't me who said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the same Taso Enes, who was a colonel, was later a Muslim general, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he's a Muslim or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that Enes is a Serbian name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to think anything. I don't know whether he's a Muslim or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know, for example, that even during the NATO aggression in 1999, and for a longer time also, not only then, he was at the head of the military security service, one of the most sensitive positions, especially in wartime, that this was a Hungarian, Farkas?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many other important posts were held by people who were not of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you're saying all this when I did not say that the army was being cleansed of foreign cadres. These were not my words. That's not what I said. That was said by a man who had paramilitary formations, who was a friend of yours; Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Dulovic, that Vojislav Seselj was my opponent, not my friend.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he's writing to you, he's your friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wrote a letter in connection with your testimony. He feels it's his duty to put that forward, so I wouldn't conclude what you just did. You mention a telegram that you adduced here. Do some things mentioned in that telegram indicate that there was a legal and, I would say, correct behaviour of the army in relation to things you mention? For example, this is a telegram which you say -- it says here: "Lieutenant Colonel Milan Remija. He says activities and phenomena having a positive effect on morale in the units of the division, and among others, he mentions proper treatment of prisoners. Does this indicate that there was an atmosphere in the army which meant that treating prisoners properly had a positive effect on morale in the army and that the army was nurturing proper behaviour toward those they were at war with? Do you think that this confirms what I'm saying or not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to explain this text, this telegram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you provided it, so I suppose you had some intention when you did that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My intention was to produce it for anyone who -- for people to estimate whose job it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He suggests certain measures to improve morale, and the first thing he mentions - these are bullets rather than numbers - but the first one is that there should be an organised effort to disarm paramilitary units, especially Dusan Silni, the Chetniks, and Arkan's soldiers, and that the organs of the Republic of Serbia should be involved in this. Do you feel that this suggestion is also a manifestation of a proper attitude which the JNA had toward phenomena that you say you observed in the field?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to put forward various opinions or interpretations of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It should be noted for the record that the accused is referring to Exhibit 342, tab 11. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says number 11 here, Mr. May, it's after this, but I suppose that you have better records than I do. I usually don't get it so tidy. It's number 10 in my file, but I assume there's no danger of confusion, because there's only one telegram here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you are speaking only of what you saw, Mr. Dulovic, but do you remember that on the road, not only at the border of Serbia, at the border of Serbian territory, but also in the depth of the territory, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you were able to see a large number of police checkpoints stopping and searching vehicles, searching for weapons or anything that might indicate looting, criminal offences, or something like that, and that this was done meticulously and that there was no road without a police checkpoint checking everybody to look for weapons, to disarm people, to arrest offenders, looking for traces of looting or criminal offences? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't pass through such checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed through a checkpoint which looked like a regular one on the Zagreb-Belgrade motorway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, Mr. Dulovic: Did you, anywhere or at any time, in Serbia, see any kind of paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where I could see them in Belgrade. In Belgrade, I did not, and I don't know what unit is a paramilitary one and what isn't, and whether they were armed or not. What I said was that these people received weapons once they were in the field, when they were far away from the place they had come from. That's when they were issued weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You told us about the events that took place in front the Visegrad hotel when an officer of the Yugoslav army, the JNA, rather, arrested somebody who had broken down the door of the hotel and stormed the hotel, somebody who, in your opinion, was a member of some paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything at all that the army did which was not proper and in keeping with the rules of service or military discipline and conduct which you could point a finger at?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, for example, Mr. Dulovic? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Trpinjska Road, I saw a tank. On the sides of the turret, there were skis, several pairs of skis, and this was absurd. That's just a small example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. As you described having seen a dead old man outside Visegrad, near some kind of river, water, was it the Drina or whatever --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the River Drina, but yes, I did see a person like that. He had his hands tied behind his back. He had some sort of cloth over his mouth. He was on the bank. And there were some reservists there, amongst them a doctor from Uzice Pozega whom I talked to. That corpse was lying there 30 metres away from us. And I asked who that was and what had happened, and he said the man had been strangled. He was a Muslim. I asked how --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why are you asking me, then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to ask you whether you had seen this old man who had been strangled. All right. Well, I assume that the doctor could have ascertained whether he had been strangled, so if one questions that kind of observation. But let me ask you this: This happened outside Visegrad. Was there another body found, that of some man, and nobody knew how he had been killed? Did you see anybody else who had been killed in all these activities that you described on your journey to Visegrad, at the entrance to Visegrad, at the exit to Visegrad, or anything like that, anything that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first time, in April, when I wanted to enter Zvornik from the other side, the opposite side, so not from the Serb side, I saw, by the Drina River, several bodies lying there. I was not able to establish whether they were men or women or anything else that could throw some light onto who they were, their ethnic group, their age, their gender, et cetera. I saw that, but that was on the other side, and the people who were on that side saw that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that. From the Serbian territory, across the Drina River, you saw several dead persons and you don't know their gender, their ethnicity, et cetera, on the banks of the river, on Bosnia-Herzegovina territory; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, when you came again on the 10th of May, that was when you saw, as far as I was able to gather from what you were saying, some tanks, artillery, in Veliki Zvornik, and then there was this notice on which it said Republika Srpska standing there.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, the army of Republika Srpska had already been established and that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had adopted a new constitution composed of Serbia and Montenegro on the 27th of April, 1992? I assume that you remember that, when that was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. What I do remember is that with the leader of a tank, the commander of a tank, on the other side, who was on the bridge, on the Muslim side, I talked to him when I passed by that way, Karakaj. That was him. And it was a tank belonging to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that after the proclamation of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say, after the 27th of April, an order was issued according to which all citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who were members of the Yugoslav People's Army are duty-bound to return to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I just remember what I saw and the conversations I had with people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But do you know -- are you aware of one very clear-cut fact: The existence of a great Yugoslavia, the FRY and the JNA, existed throughout the territory of Yugoslavia. Since the FRY was established, the members of that portion of the JNA who were citizens of Serbia and Montenegro, which make up the FRY, were withdrawn from the territories that were outside the FRY, just as the members who were on Serbia and Montenegro from other parts went back to their own republics? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say once again, you are now focusing on what I talked about and what I had said I had seen and heard. That's all I can talk about, what I have seen and heard. I'm not here to accuse or anything else; I'm here to testify about the things that I saw and heard. What you're talking about now, I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you have no notion of the fact that after the FRY was set up, the portion of the JNA which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given you his answer. Now, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions, Mr. May. I have adhered to the time allotted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall try not to take up more than 10 or 20 minutes, to get through my questions in that time. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dulovic, as you yourself said, from May 1991 up until November, which is six or seven months in all, with several smaller interruptions, that you were, almost throughout that time, in Eastern Slavonia and that you toured the towns and villages in the area to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that time interval, up until the permit that you obtained, the permit to tour the terrain in that area, up until that time you didn't need a permit or authorisation of any kind, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the beginning, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you were issued a permit, and we have it in tab 1, the permit is contained in tab 1, and it is issued from the 9th of October to the 9th of November, and you spent several days longer in the area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, throughout that period of time and the time when you had the permit in your hands, as well as the period you didn't need authorisation, were there any other journalists who were observers or representatives of international humanitarian organisations in the area, especially in the month prior to your obtaining a permit, when permits were not necessary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were journalists, yes. I remember that there were international -- well, actually, I think -- I can't quite remember the date, but in Borovo Selo, for instance, somebody was there. There was a foreigner there who had to meet with Goran Hadzic to sign some sort of agreement on an exchange, or rather, to organise liaison officers and future -- future agreements on a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Henri Wejnaendts was his name. He was an envoy of Mr. van den Broek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in knowing whether anybody throughout that period of time, including the month up until the 12th of November, whether anybody made it impossible for observers, journalists, foreign and domestic, to follow the events in that region of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, we were able to monitor events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was interested in learning. What I want to ask you now is this: On the 9th of October, once you had obtained your permit authorising you to go to the area, and when you arrived in the region, where was the army of Yugoslavia? How far? At what distance from the town of Vukovar or from the centre of Vukovar, for example? How far was it from there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need a map to indicate this, but, for example, between Borovo Selo -- they were actually along the edges of Borovo Selo, not as you go towards Vukovar, but the other end, the opposite end. And I'm talking about the tank unit that was stationed there. That means from Borovo Selo, you have Borovo Selo, then you have the railway line, then there's an airport, a sports airport, then you have Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was somewhere in that area. How far from town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, from town, you mean. Well, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never measured the distance. We would have to look at maps to ascertain this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the army was not in town, in the town proper?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which town?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in Vukovar. I was in Borovo Selo, in the suburbs of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how far away is that? What's the distance?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I would be guessing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move forward, Mr. Dulovic. You said yesterday that you had heard from a Yugoslav army officer which units were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did that same officer tell you which Croatian units were in Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you received authorisation and a permit to be able to see what was going on on this side, did you try and enter Vukovar or get authorisation to enter the town itself to see what was going on down there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attempt to do this. A colleague of mine did, however. He was a correspondent for the Vecernje Novosti newspaper. He tried from Trpinjska Cesta, from the Trpinje Road, to access the area. He started out, but he was killed later on. They found his body. In other words, you could not enter Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the man who tried to enter was killed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed by the territorials of Vrsadin [phoen]. There was a lot of shooting going on there. Everybody was shooting at everybody else. There was a lot of fear. Nobody knew who was who in the camouflage uniforms, civilian clothing, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you know that he was killed by the territorials and not by somebody else, a bullet from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lieutenant of the tank unit, Borisa Doknic, told me that, and several other officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Dulovic, when the army was quite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a long way from the centre of Vukovar, in the suburbs, were attempts made to find a peaceful solution and to stop the conflict, to prevent any other victims falling?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it. There were attempts of that kind, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to move on, this is what I'm interested in: You said that there was shooting from the town in response to the attack. When they were attacked, they responded and fired. Now, I'm interested in knowing how strong this shooting was. Was it the same as the attack? Was the shooting of equal intensity on both sides or was it stronger from one side?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is difficult to assess. I was observing the situation from the very edge of Borovo Selo, across the railway line. There were several of us there, and we were observing what was going on. We saw our tanks, Serbian tanks, that is to say, move towards Borovo Naselje - this is even closer to Vukovar - across that airstrip, airport. There were several such tanks, ten of them perhaps. And once they had moved in the direction of the airport, the Croats used mortars and started shelling. Quite a lot of people lost their lives from this mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, there were no civilians in attacks of this kind, where you have tanks moving forward. They were soldiers. They were reservists, or whoever they were, I don't really know. But the attack was stopped. They responded by mortar fire, and it was the infantrymen following the tanks that were the casualties. Some of the tanks came across mines too, so they were stopped. The whole lot of them returned, the attack was aborted. And once they had withdrawn, once our forces had withdrawn, the mortar fire stopped. So that is one example of what things looked like over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that what it was like every time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every time. It was two or three times. Actually, attempts -- two attempts of that kind were made. When Badza turned up, the commander of the Territorial Defence, as I heard from people, he issued orders that this kind of offensive should not be launched any more because there were always casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in what you said earlier on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony previously, you said that grenades were thrown. What kind were they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly mortar fire from Vukovar, because that was the most effective way. I don't know what they had. They didn't have any artillery pieces of any large calibre with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us roughly, perhaps, in this response to attacks, when they were shooting from Vukovar, how many soldiers fell victim? How many soldiers were killed, at least as far as you were able to see and judge?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not even an approximation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it appears that it was right, what Sljivancanin was saying from the tape, that young men, young soldiers, were being killed. That is not being challenged at all. That is indisputable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tapuskovic, there's no misunderstanding, as I understand the position, what Sljivancanin was doing was preventing the Red Cross to get into the hospital. And of course, it was from the hospital that people were being removed. That's the real thrust of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going into that. You heard Sljivancanin say during that conversation that young people were being killed. I wanted the Trial Chamber to find out that this fire that came in response from Vukovar killed a lot of young soldiers. I want you, Your Honours, to understand that, that shells were fired from there, and gunfire came from that direction. I don't know about all the rest that has to do with Sljivancanin. Sljivancanin said young men are being killed, so that is correct. In that fire that came by way of a response, a lot of young soldiers were killed, and Witness Dulovic mentioned it yesterday, and I think it is noteworthy and that's why I'm referring to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Even if so, what happened thereafter at Ovcara, of course really can't be justified, if true, as alleged, by the killing of soldiers, can it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am one of the persons who is profoundly convinced, certainly, just as you are convinced, that this was not justified. I am equally convinced. But one has to know what actually happened in Vukovar before that as well, what it all looked like and how people were being killed there, perhaps for nothing. And then it led to this, which certainly did happen. I'm not trying to challenge that in any way. This is an atrocity that all citizens of Yugoslavia took as very bad news. I have to assure you of that. But you should realise what was going on as the army was approaching Vukovar. That has to be known if you want to have a valid overview of the entire problem. Nobody is challenging what happened in Ovcara, let alone I, as an amicus. So this should be discussed in a proper manner now, all of it. Your Honours, Witness Dulovic testified here he was in that area for six months, perhaps even more. I'm interested in the following: Is it possible that Witness Dulovic does not know -- well, yes, I accept that there were casualties amongst the Croats. Nobody is challenging that either. But is it possible that he doesn't know anything about this, since he was there as a reporter, that other people were being killed as well? I'm not going to refer to their ethnicity. Never mind. But it wasn't only Croats who were being killed. There were all sorts of things going on over there. Well, that is what I wanted to ask Mr. Dulovic. Is it possible that he did not know what happened to the Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The official sources at that time did not wish to talk about this, which was logical. As you say, yes, people were being killed, but that would not have sounded very good. That was somebody's assessment. Namely, the number of these victims, casualties, was not accessible, nor did any official sources provide such information to the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were there on the ground. You interviewed many people. You talked about many people. You found out about many Croatian victims. Is it possible that you did not find anything out about any other victims of other ethnicities? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Victims, during the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the six months that preceded the siege of Vukovar, from May to October.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I could not find out about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm also interested about the Bosnian side. You say that you spent a month there. You explained that, that you were in Bosnia for a month. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there twice in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you also talked to people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in Zvornik that was under the control of the territorials in Bosnia. Could you go to the territory that was controlled by the Muslim forces at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know under whose control it was, but in Zvornik itself, the forces that were in Zvornik did not allow people to go beyond, to other villages outside Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to conclude now. This is my last question. I don't want to keep the Trial Chamber any longer. Is it possible that you did not hear anything? You're a journalist. You talk to people and you did not go there to resolve the kind of conflict that you described, but you went there to find out what was going on over there. You talked about a mosque that was destroyed. You talked about casualties among the Muslims. You did not say a word about rumours -- no, not about rumours, but you did not talk to people about whether there were any victims among the Serbs as well. Do you know anything about that? Were there any victims among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask about this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People told me about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any longer. I think that I published that, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome. Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 1. And while that's being done: Mr. Dulovic, Mr. Milosevic asked you about the period of time for which you had authorisation to be in Vukovar, and I want to ask you: Did you get an extension of the dates on -- of the permit that you produced here in Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that the usher just remain there. We'll ask that this be put on the overhead.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was that extension indicated on that permit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this expired, I went somewhere in town, or I can't remember any longer, but I went to the press bureau of the army, and I found the man who was in charge of permits. He's a major. I think his name was Popovic. He wrote here that the permit continues to be valid, that is to say, for a longer period of time, longer than what it says up here, between the 9th of October and further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that the usher place that on the overhead, and if you could use the pointer, just indicate where that was noted on the permit. I'd ask that it be slid up some.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're pointing to the lower left-hand portion of the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says, "The permit continues to be valid," and then, in brackets, "It is accepted from the order issued by the federal Secretariat of National Defence," and here is a signature of the major. It says "Major" and then his signature, and then there's a stamp. And that is how I managed to stay on for a longer period of time without any deadline. This is 923, that's the military post code, and this is another one. So there are two stamps, as a matter of fact. So I went to two official military posts where I received this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dulovic, during this time period, you had other permits. You had more than just the two permits that you have produced here in Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about whether or not you had a permit to be in Zvornik on the 10th of April of 1992. Had you secured authorisation before travelling to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time you were in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first tried to enter Zvornik; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. When you tried to enter Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a permit then too, but at that time, nothing helped. It was not possible to enter Zvornik. Quite simply, they did not let people cross the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you had ever been impeded from performing your duties as a journalist. Did you consider the refusal of being allowed into Zvornik despite the permit, did you consider that an impediment to fulfilling your duties?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Perhaps I could recall this now, but there were places where no permits were valid, or rather, even with a permit, one could not look at something, talk to someone, enter a certain locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there other places that you are personally aware of that, despite having a permit, you were impeded from entering an area where the Yugoslav army was present?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I can't remember. Vukovar, and this in Zvornik, the first time. I really cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, the next area that I want to inquire about is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Milosevic asked you about whether you had ever witnessed the JNA doing something which you deemed improper, and you talked about an observation you made regarding a tank. I want to recall your attention to the area of Visegrad. At the time that you were in Visegrad, first at the fortification of the Yugoslav army and then in the town, did you form an impression about whether the Yugoslav army could have entered the town earlier than it did?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when I arrived there, I said that the town looked almost like a ghost town. I saw only one person doing some digging in his garden, and I had the impression that the town was empty. I found this a bit strange. The army was there, there was a military presence, and now they were supposed to enter town and fight, and enter a town that had been abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that Mr. Dulovic be shown Defence Exhibit 56 and I ask that it be turned to the last page so he can see the signature of the person on that last page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I'd ask you to look at the signature and the name of that person on the last page. I'd ask you to read it for us.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The district public attorney, public prosecutor, Branko Njegovan. I talked to him in Sabac. I interviewed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the interview that you conducted with this prosecutor, is it contained on the videotape we saw a portion of, Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 13, the Yellow Wasp video?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the question you put to Mr. Njegovan during the course of your interview with him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that interview a long time ago. It was relatively short, but I really cannot remember what I asked him. Perhaps there were several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 13, page 14. I apologise. I'm sorry, page 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm showing -- asking you to take a look at a transcript of the interview. I'd ask you to read it and see if that refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it the same page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian and the English are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at 24 and then go on to 25.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bottom of page 24 and then going on to page 25. Can you see the heading "Branko Njegovan"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection regarding the interview that you had with the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at this first page, or rather, there seems to be a constant mistake here throughout. It says "Jovan Duljic," and my name is Dulovic, and this is me. Yes. Yes, I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you summarise for us what the prosecutor told you -- or, I'm sorry. I return to my original question: What question did you put to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I had in my hands the indictment that had been issued against the Vuckovic brothers. I asked the prosecutor why there was no mention in the indictment of the transfer of civilians from the settlement of Divice in Celopek, where the cultural centre was and where civilians from Celopek were detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also ask him why none of the survivors were called at the trial of these two men?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Yes. Yes. Now I remember. There were no witnesses whatsoever who would give evidence about what Vuckovic did. Dusan Vuckovic, nicknamed Repic. There was a guard there who was heard, I think, but not in Sabac. This man did not want to come as a witness at all when Dusan Vuckovic -- to testify, rather, about the killing of 17 civilians at the cultural centre in Celopek, when Repic did that. He didn't want to testify about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- my question to you is, more specifically: What did the prosecutor tell you was the reason why he did not call any of the survivors at the trial of these two men?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly, he could not get in touch with them, as far as I can remember. Perhaps it's somewhere in here, so I'd like to have a look at it. But he could not get in touch with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I draw your attention to page 25, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also speak with one of the survivors who expressed to you that they were willing to come or were willing to give evidence on videotape but that they had not been contacted again by Mr. Njegovan?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just remember my conversation with an architect, Himza Tulic. In Zvornik, he was in charge of the town planning institution. I talked to him in Austria. He told me about this, about all the crimes in Zvornik, and he mentioned the Vuckovic brothers and many others, both victims and criminals, by name. I can't really -- I have to have a look at this. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I think we have the gist of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, the last couple of questions I have for you regarding the large numbers of crimes, very horrific descriptions of crimes that Mr. Milosevic has put to you and asked you whether you are aware of them as being part of the context of the time you were there and the crimes that you gave some information regarding, and my question for you is the following: During the entire time you were in 81 Ulica Nova in the presence of the JNA, of the Vukovar, Territorial Defence, of Seselj's men, of other paramilitaries, did you hear any of these people in that place you've described as a command centre, did you hear any of these people talking about the crimes and the atrocities that Mr. Milosevic has put to you here today?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they did not tell me about it at the time. I don't remember. That wouldn't surprise me, though, because this is a part of Vukovar that is called Sajmiste and that has a Serb population. They were there all the time, and according to what they had said, the Croats had never come there and had had no interventions in that area, Sajmiste. Ulica Nova 81 belongs to that area as well. Now, whether they knew about this or did not is something I don't know, but I don't remember that they told me about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you interviewed Serbs that had been trapped in Vukovar, did the course of those interviews, did they ever describe for you some of the atrocities Mr. Milosevic has described as being committed against Serbs? Did they ever describe those types of atrocities to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I'm sure they didn't. They didn't describe the things Mr. Milosevic mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This issue of a conversation with the prosecutor and so on and so forth was not touched upon during the examination-in-chief, and in view of this, I would like to ask the witness a few questions about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It arose from what you -- the document that you put in to the witness, and on the whole, we have to have a rule which means that examination has to come to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will make an exception on this occasion, and you can ask questions, but you've got two minutes to do it, two or three minutes at the most. I'm not going to let you have a free-ranging examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't intend to ask all the questions I would wish to ask. I just want to clarify a certain point in relation to this trial. Further cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you were a journalist reporting on court proceedings for a long time, I assume you are aware of the fact that the authorities in Serbia and in Yugoslavia, then as now, respected the division of power, and that there is executive, legislative, and judicial power, the judiciary. Are you aware of this, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on paper only. The judiciary was never independent, and neither was the legislative branch of government. Everything was controlled by the executive government, as you know well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this particular case, did the police, which is the executive branch, arrest the perpetrators, submit information showing that he had killed 17 people, then four others, that previously he had tortured them, and did they not hand them over to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And unfortunately, there were no witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I'm asking you only one thing: As I know that there is no president of a chamber or a judge in Yugoslavia who could ever say that there had been any interventions telling him how to judge, do you think that the executive branch of government completed their task when they arrested this man and handed him over, along with all the information and the charges contained in the indictment, they handed him over to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public prosecutors in Serbia, during the reign of the accused, were absolutely linked to politics and to what they were told by the executive branch of government; whom to prosecute, whom not to prosecute, whether to issue an indictment or not, and the accused knows this full well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, if we were to accept your assumption --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an assumption. For years I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the public prosecutor in this case submit an indictment? Did he issue an indictment? You say they were told whether to do so or not. Did they issue an indictment, and does the indictment say that this man tortured people, that he killed 17 people, that later on he killed another four, that he was charged with this and handed over to the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the last question. Yes, Mr. Dulovic. Do you want to reply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do wish to reply. This trial, Your Honours, was the most shameful thing I had ever seen in more than 40 years. This was unprecedented. For example, at that trial, there was a witness, a Muslim woman who had been raped by this man Repic. She had to answer, weeping, before the Court, to all the shameless questions put to her by the presiding judge as to the manner in which the rape took place, with every detail, whereas under the Criminal Code in our country, rape trials are held in closed session and the public is thought to be undesirable. In this case, the public gallery was full, and this woman had to answer, in shameful detail, as to how she was raped. This is the sort of judiciary Mr. Milosevic is talking about. She had to appear in court for about three times and tell the same story over and over again. I want to tell you that this woman who was a victim was humiliated, was horribly humiliated. That's what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We simply cannot go on in this way. You've asked your questions. Mr. Dulovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we begin, some of the witnesses -- or a portion of the witness's testimony which is most directly relevant to the indictment begins on paragraph 8. I believe it would be appropriate to take the rest of it in more summary fashion, and with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Court's permission, would propose to lead him through the first few paragraphs of his proposed testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. When you get to anything likely to be controversial, do it in the normal way, but of course lead him through the non-controversial matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As we start, I would ask to go into private session to ask him his name and a couple of biographical details that may come up in the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the record, his name for these purposes should be given too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's C-1141, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-1141, I want to ask you to tell us how many different villages make up the municipality of Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: The former municipality of Hrvatska Dubica. Why "former"? Because when I came to Hrvatska Dubica, the municipality was dissolved and it fell under Hrvatska Kostajnica. However, within the former municipality, there were four villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the names of those villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Zivaja, Cerovljani, Bacin, Slabinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which of those villages were predominantly occupied by Croat people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Bacin and Cerovljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which ones were primarily occupied by Serb people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Zivaja and Slabinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there one place in Hrvatska Dubica that was approximately 50/50 between Serbs and Croats, approximately half Croat, half Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the village of Hrvatska Dubica itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to 1990, how would you characterise the relationship between Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: In brief, or do you want me to describe it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, in brief, quite normal. Everybody lived together in harmony. There was no hatred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when you noticed a change in this in Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: In 1990, after the multiparty elections had been held. It was then that more than one party appeared in Dubica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that as the relationship between the two ethnic communities deteriorated, that both sides began to arm themselves and mobilise for a possible conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when paramilitaries from the Republic of Serbia arrived in Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I left it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave it? Just a date at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: On the 13th of September, the bridge in Hrvatska Dubica was blown up. I think on the 14th of September, which was a Thursday, I learned about what had happened. I took my wife to Zagreb, and then I stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which year? Can we determine that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we speaking about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After bringing your wife to Zagreb, did you return to Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't take her to Zagreb. I sent her there and I stayed on at home. And on that Thursday, Friday, and Saturday evening, I was there. Then I went about two kilometres further away, to a hamlet near Dubica, where a friend of mine lived, someone who had been a colleague of mine at the school. I went there on a motorcycle. When I arrived at his house, I found him there, and his father, and an elderly woman whom I didn't know. They were getting ready to go and loading something onto a tractor. I asked them what was going on, and they said they had to leave. I left my motorcycle in the basement of his house, and together with him, his father, and that elderly woman, I got on the tractor and we went off in the direction of Kutina, under cover of night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time after this point in time that you returned to Hrvatska Dubica through Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: On the 2nd of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have previously described for us that the bridge was blown up. Can you describe the condition of the bridge when you returned on this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: One side had been destroyed, but you could cross the bridge because they had put something there, some kind of boulders or broad planks, something of that kind. So you could go up and down these planks and cross that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this time when you returned to your village, do you see armed forces in and around the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Not in the village, but outside the village there were some there, towards the Sava River. About four or five kilometres away there's a forest -- actually, it's Cerovljani and Zivaja, those two places, and from Jesenice onwards. That's where the woods start. So it's a real forest, actually. And then you have the Sava River. And that's where the front line was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see members of the Yugoslav People's Army as part of these armed forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I saw reservists, and they were wearing the grey-green type of uniform. They were reservists, and I knew some of them because they were locals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were reservists of the Yugoslav People's Army? You need to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the SAO Krajina police present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any paramilitary forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Apart from those reservists, and apart from those policemen, I didn't see anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the headquarters of the police -- of the SAO Krajina police were in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. It was in the old school building. We've got a new school building now, but this was in the old building, in the old school, and that's where an agricultural cooperative was set up as well. Anyway, it's the old school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point in time, who is the commander of the local police brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I don't really know -- actually, there were two of them, two men. One was Veljko Radunovic, and the other was his son, Stevo. I would say that they were the two main people in charge of that. Nobody told me, but I think that they were in command, and I knew both of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I think we ought to establish whether a local brigade of the police force existed, because a brigade is a very large formation for such a small place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, you can ask about that when it's your turn. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-1141, can you tell us about how many members made up the local police force in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: About 30. 31 or 32, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the 20th of October, 1991. Do you recall where you were that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I remember, yes. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the day of the week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: It was a Sunday, Sunday morning, about half past 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you went to a neighbour's house to borrow a cup of milk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What occurred while you were in your neighbour's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: While the old woman was pouring some milk for me in her home, her daughter was outside in the yard, and she suddenly rushed into the house --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she say anything when she entered the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: And when she came in, she said to me, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you not to mention any nickname or any other personal identifying information in open session. Did you go outside your neighbour's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: When I came up to the door, the door of my house, the entrance door, on the fence, actually, the iron fence, I saw a young man standing there, waiting for me. It was raining, so he had a sort of rain cloak over him. There was a truck standing behind him. And he asked me if that was my house. I said yes, it was. And he said, "Well, get ready, because we're going off to the fire brigade building for a meeting there."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-1141, could you tell us: Was there anything written on the side of the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, there was. What it said was "Milicija SAO Krajina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the man who you just described to us spoke to you, were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there any other men present at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes. There was another person, the driver of the truck, who was in the truck. He was a young man, who did the driving. Did either of these men have uniforms on, that you could tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: As it was raining, the one that met me, who wasn't in the truck, was wearing this sort of rain cloak, something of that nature. I didn't see the other one, whether he was in uniform or not, because he was sitting inside the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the man said, "Well, get ready, because we're going off to the fire brigade building for a meeting," what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I went inside the house to put something on. I took a jacket, my cap, and went outside. I locked the door to the house and the gate and went into the truck. I said that I could come on foot, because I knew the way, and he said, "Never mind. It's raining. It's best that you come in the truck with us, so that's what I did. I got up into the truck. There were four old women there, and they were sitting on a sort of wooden bench or something like that. The truck had a canvas awning over it because it was raining. And right after that, my neighbour turned up, the one that had given me the milk, and she was accompanied by her daughter. Some other neighbours turned up too: A woman and her husband, both of them were pensioners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say they turned up, did they also enter the rear of the truck, where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No, they didn't get up on their own. They were assisted up. The soldier helped them get up onto the truck, helped these old women to get up onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when the truck left the area by your house and travelled somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No. When we got into the truck, the truck started off, and on the way to the fire brigade station, it stopped at several points, and every time it stopped, people would get onto the truck; old men and women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before you arrived at the fire station, approximately how many people were in the rear of the truck with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I counted about 23 of us who had been boarded up onto the truck and who got out at the fire station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of the other people that were in the truck, did you recognise them as being other people who lived in the same area as yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were all from Dubica. Of course I knew them. I taught their children and grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the fire station, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: We got off the truck. It was still raining. And we stood outside in front of the fire station, under the edge of the roof. And after five or perhaps ten minutes - I can't say exactly, but very soon afterwards - a bus turned up. It had also come from Dubica. And the bus brought some old women and men, also from Dubica. There were fewer of them, perhaps about - well, I can't say exactly - 15 or 16 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time it was that you arrived at the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: It was 8.30, thereabouts, or maybe closer to 9.00. Between 8.30 and 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you entered the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: When the other lot got off, the old men and women from the bus, we stayed outside for a while, and sometime after 9.00 a woman came, and a man. They were armed. And they told us to go inside the fire station. We all went inside and we never went out again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the two people you've just described as being armed, were there any other people at that time by the fire station that had weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No. They were guards. There were three guards in two places, and they would take turns and have shifts. They were all armed. Three times two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards that you're describing now, were you able to identify their uniform, or uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Olive-green, yes, grey-green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that identify them as belonging to a particular unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what unit did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I don't know the name, but the headquarters of that unit was in Zivaja. The commander of that headquarters or that unit, or whatever it was, a battalion or whatever, but the commander was -- I don't know him personally. He was a middle-aged man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these guards, were they military personnel or police personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Military personnel, because they wore the olive-green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you approximate for us how many people altogether were in the fire station after having been collected from throughout the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Fifty-three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of what their ages were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: All of them over 60 years of age, except one person, a young boy. I think he was a boy. He was -- he had a broken leg. I don't know how he came to break it. So he couldn't walk very well. He limped a little, and his leg was in a plaster cast. He was younger. Otherwise, all the others were old people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the young boy, who was the youngest -- next youngest person in that group of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say. I don't know. I was younger than those old people there, at the time. I was then, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe approximately how many were men, how many were women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, I would say half/half. Perhaps there were more women than men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for us the ethnic make-up of that group of 53?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: There were Serbs and there were Croats and there were Muslims too. Mostly they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were the people that were gathered in the fire station, were they free to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described for us being told about the necessity of you going to the fire station for a meeting. Was a meeting ever held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, while they were rounding up the people, and when they came to my house - I'm going back a bit now - they said that we would go for a meeting and then go back, but no meeting was ever held, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that the 53 people weren't free to leave. Can you describe what specific observations you made that led you to the conclusion that you were not free to leave the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, the guard. As the guards took turns, the first lot of guards, the first two guards on duty, when they came inside, read out a list of names. Somebody had provided them with a list and they read out the names, and I counted about 53 persons on that list. I was number 53 called out. Then they went out, they locked the door, and one of the guards went one way behind the fire station and the other one stood guard in front of the station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a toilet in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. There was, but you couldn't reach it from the building. You had to go round about. You would have to have gone outside the building, round the corner, into the toilet, that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people inside the building permitted to walk freely out to the toilet and use it when they needed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I saw some people who needed to go to the toilet knock on the door, the guard would open the door, ask them what they wanted, they asked to be excused, and then he would take the person out, lock the door again. He probably took them to the lavatory around the building. And then after that, they would return. He would unlock the door, the person would come back into the room, the guard would lock the door again and leave. So if somebody asked to be excused, they would allow them to, escort them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the course of that day that you had an argument with one of the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have an argument with the guard. What happened was that I went out perhaps 5.00, half past 5.00. I knocked -- or rather, I recognised one of the guards who was on duty. He was a (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: something, but he took me out, locked the door, and we stood outside. It was raining all the time. We were standing by the staircase, under the roof. And he asked me what I wanted, and he [as interpreted] said, "Well, let me go home. I don't think there's going to be a meeting of any kind here. So it's getting dark, and can I go home? And I haven't got enough clothes on me. I'm going to be very cold if I stay around like this." He kept me there and tried to convince me not to leave, that somebody would turn up and that we would have a meeting and that we could all go home after the meeting. However, during this conversation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before you go further, I want to just establish: You said that this discussion with the guard began somewhere between 5.00 and 5.30; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you first entered the fire station at 9.00 in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 53 people that you've told us about -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: At 1730 hours, not 5.30 a.m., I mean 1730, that is to say, in the afternoon, towards evening. That was the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, during the period of time between when you first went into the fire station and when you had this discussion with the guard between 5.00 and 5.30, was the entire group of 53 people kept together in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when some of the people were allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe how many people were allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Six of them. Six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the circumstances under which they were permitted to leave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Somebody came and asked to be taken out. I saw one person. I saw one person coming. I could see this through the window. They were standing outside the station. The guard came back to look for that person, and that person was allowed to leave, and they are alive. All those six people are alive to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention back to the time of your having this argument with the guard. Did something happen during the course of that discussion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I said to the guard, "Listen here. I'm cold. If you don't let me go home, I'm going to go home of my own free will, and you can shoot after me." He began to cry, and he said, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: (redacted). And he said, "Please don't leave while I'm on duty." That meant that he was afraid and that if I left and the other shift turned up, there would be a roll-call. However, in the meantime, a car drew up. I saw the lights. And they parked about 50 metres before the fire station. They stopped in front of a building. Opposite that building was a post office, the old post office. A person got out of the car. They didn't have a cap on their head, just a sort of raincoat or cloak. I didn't know who that was. But that person made a sign. They didn't say anything, but they made a sign to the guard to call him to come up. I waited by the staircase while the guard went to see this man. He went up to the car. They had a discussion of some kind. I don't know what they were saying. The guard returned, and this is what he said: "Go up to the car. The man wants to see you." I did that. I went up to the car and I recognised -- do I have to say the name? Janjeta?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a good reason why -- do you feel you cannot say the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, no. I haven't mentioned any names so far, but there's no reason I shouldn't, no.
