utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell us: Who is the person that was at the car.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: He was also a pupil of mine, but I heard people say later on that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he might have been the guard shift leader. I don't know what he was, but that's what other people said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for just a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now, this person who was at the car, did he say anything to you regarding your being detained in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Not really. He didn't say anything about detention. But the person asked me what I had said to the guard. I said I had asked the guard to let me go home and get some warmer clothes, because night was drawing close and it was cold. And he asked me, "What else did you say to him?" I said, "Well, nothing else." And then he persisted. He said again. "What else did you say to the guard?" Because it seems that the guard told him that I had told the guard that I was going to escape, to go off on my own if he didn't let me go. And I said, "Well, I said to the guard that if he didn't allow me to go home, I would go home anyway." He told me then to get into the car, to get into the car, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he drive you somewhere in the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I got into the car and he went up to the guard. And when he returned, he got into the car and drove me off along the road leading to Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you got out of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I did not get out of the car. About a kilometre after the fire station, he turned the car around. He went back by the house, and then he went towards my house. He brought me to my house. It was night-time. He stopped the car, and he said the following to me: "Don't you dare stay at home overnight; and secondly, don't you dare ever tell anyone that you were with me if you get caught."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay at your home that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go? Without telling us the name of the person who you went to, just give us some general idea about where you went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I went into the hills. That's what we call it: The hills. Because my house is low down by the river. So I went into the hills. I didn't take the road. I went through the woods. And I reached a house. I reached the house of a person who was on very good terms with me, still is, as a matter of fact, this person is still alive. So since the lights were on in front of his house, I stopped there. And there was a cornfield right by the house, so I got out of the cornfield and I came to the fence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: With respect, we don't need too much detail of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and get the matter fairly quickly, get to the nub of this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you tried escape and you were arrested by the local police? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you held at the police station, where you were beaten and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Nothing. They interrogated me. I was there for two days and two nights, in a room. Main accusation was: Why did I escape from the fire station building, that I had some weapons at home, that I was concealing weapons, and there was another major accusation: Why I did not accept the SDS, that party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you left the area of Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, out of the original 53 people, you've described six people as having left while you were present in the fire station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you learn later that three other people were allowed to leave the fire station during the -- after you left the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to March and April of 1997. Were you present during the exhumation of a number of bodies in Bacin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that exhumation include some of the people who you were in the fire station with on the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you make a list for the Office of the Prosecutor of the people who were in the fire station who did not leave, were not part of the six or the three people that left, but the remaining -- the people that remained in the fire station? Did you create such a list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the following exhibit be marked and shown to the witness. There's only one exhibit with this witness, so there's no binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 344, under seal, confidential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to look at Prosecution Exhibit 344. It's a three-page document. Is that the list that you drafted of the people who remained in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of the ethnic make-up of the 43 people on your list who remained in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Serbs -- two Serbs, and the rest, Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge as to what happened to the 43 people on this list, some of which were exhumed from Bacin several years later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: When I managed to get out of the building on Sunday evening, they remained behind. However, early in the morning they were loaded onto a bus and they took them towards Kostajnica, taking the road. Four or five kilometres away from Dubica, in Bacin, they got them off the bus by the river and they killed all of them. All 43 were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you personally witness this or is this information you learned from other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I did not see it personally because I was on the run; I was in the hills. But across the river, in Bosnia, there is a village too, and that village is perhaps up to a kilometre away from the place where they were executed. People from that village said, and still say until the present day, that they heard gunfire and moaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I just wanted to clarify the circumstances in which the witness went on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exactly why did he go on the truck? Did he go voluntarily or was he coerced, was he forced?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified earlier that you had offered to walk to the fire station. Did you feel that you were free to walk to the fire station if you insisted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you observed or what was said to you that led you to the conclusion that you were not free, that you had to travel with these two men in the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: They said that we were going to a meeting, that we should not go on foot, and we should make sure that everyone should come, all who had stayed behind, and that this was an important meeting. So I boarded the truck. I said, "All right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the witness say why, as a person of Serb ethnicity, he was treated in that way?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard Judge Robinson's question. Do you have any idea why you, as a Serb, were treated and detained with the group of people that were predominantly Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: The main reason is my refusal, towards the end of June and beginning of July, to be president of the SDS party. In my opinion, that's the main reason. They were distributing weapons too. I could not get weapons because they were suspicious of me. Secondly, even before that, and then I objected to some kind of behaviour that was wrong, and what was being done was wrong. However, some people didn't like that, especially the leaders, and that's how they behaved to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe more specifically what behaviour you observed that you objected to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Well, against looting, against persecuting people. They did some things arbitrarily, I mean this police of the SAO Krajina, the locals, the way they call themselves, the way they introduce themselves. The people didn't really want to move about at that time. Throughout the summer, everybody was frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The particular -- sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does he know the other Serbs? Did he know the other Serbs who were brought to the fire station?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the other Serbs that were in the fire station with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And would he be able to say why they were brought there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Judge Robinson is asking: Do you know why some of these other Serbs were selected and their names were on this list and they were detained in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: I can't really say. They collected everyone. I can just say one thing, though: One person who never got dressed, or rather, did not have a uniform, that is a person who took over when I refused to be leader of the SDS. Then this younger person was appointed, and that is what he was. And then, when I succeeded, after this entire procedure, to escape to Bosanska Dubica, he saw me there, by a building called Sumarija. I was standing there, he saw me, and he walked up to me, and he talked to me. He said to me, inter alia, that he had given orders to have my name deleted from the list. And I said, "Why only me? Why was this list made at all?" So I came to the conclusion that he had known that the list had been prepared, and all people who were on this list were taken to the fire brigade building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd like to ask some questions about the ten people who were released other than yourself. Were they all Serbs, or Croats included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both Croats and Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you in the position to tell us as to the reason why they were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. Somebody came to pick them up. Who it was, I don't know. And it wasn't all at once; it happened during the course of the day. I can give an example, an example that I saw. A person came, a Serb who was married to a Croat woman. His wife had a brother. He had a bit of a hump. He was a cleaner, a street cleaner, in Bosanska Dubica. He took that wife's brother out. He's alive Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. until the present day. And so on and so forth. A young man also came and took out a waitress. She was a waitress in a restaurant. I saw that too. I didn't see the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on Prosecution Exhibit 344, the list of the 43 people that were ultimately killed, how many names on that list, or how many people on that list were something other than Croat? And please feel free to look at the exhibit in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If my memory is correct, he said there were two Serbs among 43 people. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you speak the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Here it is. Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination on Monday morning. We'll not start now. Mr. Milosevic, you'll have an hour to cross-examine, the same as you had for the other crime-base witnesses in the other part of the trial, and slightly more than the Prosecution had. But that's on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I am going to cross-examine this witness too, but doesn't it seem quite absurd to you to have such witnesses brought here to testify in connection with the indictment brought against me? What do I have to do with this, and what does Serbia have to do with all the events that this witness described here? You could have brought anybody from the street --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear you in argument in due course, but there's no need to be offensive about the witness at all. If you agree with the statement and you don't want the witness to be called, you can always do so. You can always simply agree that the statement be part of the evidence, and that will save a great deal of time for everybody. However, if you wish to cross-examine, then of course in certain circumstances you may do so. There is, as you know, a rule which allows us to admit a statement without cross-examination. But there's no call to be offensive about the witness. Witness C-1141, as you're called, would you be back, please, on Monday morning. I think the time is half past 9.00. I'm told it is. So would you be back then. Could you remember, during this adjournment, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. No, Mr. Milosevic. We're going to adjourn now. Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday,, the 21st day of October 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
